text: Slavery was central to Confederate secession and the Civil War. The Union initially fought to preserve the nation; emancipation became a major Union war aim.
source: NPS - Slavery and the Civil War

text: Union and Confederate cavalry gathered information about opposing armies. Scouting helped commanders learn where enemy forces were moving before choosing deployments.
Cavalry protected marching infantry, guarded supply wagons, and raided supplies behind opposing lines.
Cavalry mobility depended on healthy horses and enough feed and water. Supply problems could limit even a fast-moving force.
Both armies used wig-wag signaling. Soldiers moved flags or torches in coded patterns where telegraph wires were unavailable.
source: NPS - An Innovative Technology of War

text: Signal officers encrypted messages using rotating disks matching letters to numbers. Changing alignment changed the code.
source: NPS - An Innovative Technology of War

text: Mountains and rivers complicated communication at Harpers Ferry. Signal flags connected commanders, but messages took time and fog interfered.
Confederate defenses at Centreville included fake cannons called Quaker guns. March 1862 photographs show mounted logs used to deceive observers.
Corinth, Mississippi was strategically important because two railroads crossed there. The junction affected movement of troops and supplies.
Union troops at Gettysburg established a curved defensive line along ridges and hills, defending high ground on the second and third days.
On Gettysburg's second day, Union commanders moved reinforcements from quieter positions to threatened ones, helping stop attacks on their left.
After direct assaults failed at Vicksburg, Grant changed approach. Union troops surrounded the city, cutting outside supplies and communications.
Union plans included blockading the coast, advancing through the Mississippi valley, and capturing Richmond; strategy connected widely separated operations.
The Union blockade aimed to restrict Confederate overseas trade and supplies. Blockade-running ships tried slipping past Union vessels.
source: NPS - Fort Morgan and Mobile Bay

text: Union success at Mobile Bay in 1864 closed the port to blockade runners; the city remained Confederate-held into 1865, illustrating controlling access as an objective.
source: NPS - Fort Morgan and Mobile Bay

text: At Fort Donelson, Ulysses S. Grant reasoned that the Confederate breakout attack had weakened another part of their line. He ordered Charles F. Smith to attack there; Smith captured defensive works, and surrender talks followed the next morning.
source: NPS - Smith's Attack at Fort Donelson

text: At Jonesborough, William T. Sherman moved six infantry corps against Atlanta's railroad supply lines instead of relying on small raids. Union troops defeated the defenders and cut the railroad, forcing John Bell Hood to evacuate Atlanta, although Hardee's Confederate command escaped.
lesson: Commit enough force against a vital supply route.

text: At Nashville, George H. Thomas ordered a diversion against the Confederate right while concentrating his main force against the left. His troops captured the outer defenses; renewed pressure on the left the next day broke Hood's army and forced its retreat.
lesson: Use a diversion to support a concentrated attack.
source: NPS - Battle of Franklin Special Resource Study: Nashville

text: At Cedar Creek, Philip Sheridan reorganized his retreating army into a long battle line with cavalry on both ends. During the counterattack, Union troops outflanked the Confederate left, and cavalry exploited the opening to turn the Confederate retreat into a rout.

At Gettysburg, George G. Meade used interior lines to move troops from quieter positions to threatened parts of his army. These reinforcements helped repair the Union line on July 2, preserving the defense that ultimately defeated Lee's attacks.
lesson: Move reserves efficiently to threatened positions.
source: US Army Center of Military History - Gettysburg Campaign, p.60

text: At Pea Ridge, Samuel R. Curtis coordinated an artillery bombardment with a synchronized infantry advance. His troops recovered ground lost the previous day and pushed back the Confederate line, helping turn a difficult defensive battle into a Union victory.
lesson: Coordinate different forces toward one objective.
source: American Battlefield Trust - Battle of Pea Ridge

text: At Chancellorsville, Robert E. Lee kept troops facing the Union army while Thomas 'Stonewall' Jackson marched around its exposed right flank. Jackson's surprise attack drove the Union XI Corps from the field, an important Confederate success during the battle.
lesson: Fix attention in front while maneuvering around a flank.

text: At Second Manassas, James Longstreet waited while Union attacks focused on Jackson's defensive line. When the Union formations became disorganized, Longstreet launched a large attack against their exposed left flank, helping force Pope's army to withdraw across Bull Run.
lesson: Time an attack against an exposed flank.

text: At Chickamauga, James Longstreet launched an attack with three divisions stacked behind one another. By chance, Union orders had just opened a gap in their path. The Confederate column broke through, driving major Union formations from the field.
lesson: Concentrated force can exploit an unexpected gap.
source: NPS Civil War Series archive - Chickamauga

text: At Port Republic, Thomas 'Stonewall' Jackson sent Richard Taylor's brigade against the Union artillery position called the Coaling. After earlier attacks failed, Taylor attacked again with reinforcements. Capturing the guns' position forced the rest of the Union line to withdraw.
lesson: Reinforce an attack on a key position.

text: At Second Winchester, Richard S. Ewell sent Jubal Early on a wide march to attack West Fort while other troops maintained pressure south of town. The fort fell; Confederate troops also blocked a retreat route, helping turn the Union withdrawal into defeat.
lesson: Combine a flank attack with control of retreat routes.

text: At Fredericksburg, James Longstreet's defense combined infantry behind the Sunken Road's stone wall with artillery on the heights above. The guns could fire over the infantry at approaching Union formations, helping the defenders repel repeated attacks and win a tactical victory.
lesson: Combine protected positions with supporting fire.
